atoms.text: The term Aboriginal Australians refers to various distinct peoples who have inhabited the continent for over 65,000 years. Each people lived on their own land and organised their individual law, religion, trade-network as well as inter-cultural relationships. The process of the self-identification of Aboriginal Peoples as a single group only started 200 years ago after Australia was colonised by Europeans. The picture shows the Australian Aboriginal Flag.

atoms.a: In some areas Aboriginal Australians lived in semi-permanent villages, most usually in less arid areas. Most Aboriginal communities were semi-nomadic, moving in a regular cycle over a defined territory, following seasonal food sources and returning to the same places at the same time each year. In the more arid areas Aboriginal Australians were nomadic, ranging over wide areas in search of food resources.

atoms.a: Food was not found without effort. In some areas men and women had to spend more than half of the day obtaining food. Larger animals and birds, such as kangaroos and emus, were hunted with a boomerang or stone. The men were excellent trackers and stalkers, approaching their prey running where there was bush, or crawling when in the open field. They were careful to stay downwind and sometimes covered themselves with mud to disguise their smell.

atoms.text: In 1788 the colonisation of Australia by British settlers started. Many Aboriginal People were then dispossessed of their land and even forcibly removed. Additionally, the European people brought diseases like smallpox which killed numerous Aboriginal People. During the period between 1905 and 1970 the Australian government removed thousands of Aboriginal children of mixed descent from their families to be raised by white foster families and assimilate to white society. The children affected by this cruel act are called the Stolen Generations.

atoms.text: Today, only about three percent of Australia's population identify as Aboriginal Australians - about 600,000 people on the continent. Only a small number of the Aboriginal Peoples still live in the Outback. The majority of them live, like most other Australians, in urban areas leading a modern life. The former spirituality and connection to nature has mostly been abandoned. Unfortunately, many Aboriginal Australians have to deal with extreme poverty and unemployment. However, there are still people who preserve and teach about old traditions and religions or try to improve the situation for Aboriginal Australians politically.
